claim: In 2017 recurrent networks (LSTMs, GRUs) were, in the Transformer paper's own first words, 'firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation', and attention was used 'in conjunction with a recurrent network' in 'all but a few cases'.

Per Wired's oral history, in 2016 Jakob Uszkoreit suggested self-attention to Illia Polosukhin over lunch in a Google cafe for a fast question-answering problem; Uszkoreit, Polosukhin and Ashish Vaswani wrote a design document titled 'Transformers: Iterative Self-Attention and Processing for Various Tasks', which ended with a cartoon of six Transformers zapping lasers in mountainous terrain.

Wired reports the design-doc trio (Uszkoreit, Polosukhin, Vaswani) picked the name 'transformers' from 'day zero' because the mechanism transforms the information it takes in; Uszkoreit's two childhood Transformer toys were an added reason, not the sole one.

Illia Polosukhin, born in Ukraine, left Google in early 2017 before the paper was finished and co-founded NEAR, a blockchain company and the only one of the eight authors' companies not built on transformers.

Per Wired, 'one day in 2017' Noam Shazeer, at Google since 2000, overheard Vaswani and Niki Parmar while passing Lukasz Kaiser's workspace in Building 1965, joined, and rewrote the code; Uszkoreit said that until then the model, compared with LSTMs, 'wasn't better'. Wired gives no season.

Facebook AI Research's convolutional ConvS2S translation model (arXiv 1705.03122, 8 May 2017) was the number the Google team was trying to beat; Parmar recalled it had taken Facebook days to train and the Transformer a matter of hours.

The team worked in Google's Buildings 1945 and 1965 on Charleston Road, Mountain View, gravitating to 1965 because 'it had a better espresso machine in the micro-kitchen'; a second-floor room in 1965 had couches by a curtain whose pattern looked to Vaswani like synapses and neurons.

The New Yorker reports that at about 3 a.m. during the late sprint Vaswani told Aidan Gomez the work was 'going to be a huge deal' and 'bigger' than machine translation, while Gomez thought 'It's just machine translation'; this is remembered dialogue, not a transcript. The team was 'pushing flat out for twelve weeks'.

A couple of weeks before the deadline Parmar and Vaswani learned in the Google lobby that the model had passed 26 BLEU and phoned Uszkoreit, who was driving down from paragliding; Wired says he broke out an old bottle of champagne from his mountain expedition truck. Parmar's only quoted words are 'Jakob had some old champagne in his car.'

The NIPS 2017 paper deadline was Friday 19 May 2017, 20:00 UTC. Parmar recalled the English-French numbers came 'like, five minutes before we submitted'; Wired's narration says the paper went in 'with barely two minutes to spare'.

Llion Jones, born and raised in Wales, coined the title 'Attention Is All You Need' from the Beatles' 'All You Need Is Love': 'It literally took five seconds of thought. I didn't think they would use it.'

'Attention Is All You Need' (arXiv 1706.03762) was posted on 12 June 2017, submitted by Llion Jones, by eight Google authors (Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin), and presented at NIPS 2017 in Long Beach, California; revisions ran to v7 (2 August 2023).

The paper's author footnote reads 'Equal contribution. Listing order is random.' and assigns roles: Uszkoreit proposed replacing RNNs with self-attention; Vaswani with Polosukhin designed and implemented the first Transformer models; Shazeer proposed scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention and the parameter-free position representation; Parmar designed, implemented, tuned and evaluated countless variants; Jones built the initial codebase, efficient inference and visualizations; Kaiser and Gomez designed and implemented tensor2tensor.

Aidan Gomez was a University of Toronto undergraduate intern at Google Brain, aged 20 and too young to drink in the US; he later learned the internship was meant for PhD students. He had joined Hinton's lab as an undergraduate and grew up in an Ontario farming village where his family tapped maple trees.

The Transformer is an encoder-decoder with 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, d_model = 512, 8 attention heads of size 64, feed-forward inner size 2048, residual connections with layer normalisation (post-LN), and Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V; the base model has about 65 million parameters and the big model (d_model 1024, 16 heads, d_ff 4096) 213 million.

The paper divides dot products by sqrt(d_k) because 'for large values of d_k, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients'; its footnote notes that for unit-variance components q.k has variance d_k.

The original Transformer used fixed sinusoidal positional encodings added to the embeddings, with wavelengths forming a geometric progression from 2pi to 10000*2pi; learned position embeddings gave 'nearly identical results' (25.7 vs 25.8 dev BLEU).
In the paper's ablations (EN-DE dev BLEU, base 25.8) one head scored 24.9, 'Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting', 32 heads 25.4, no dropout 24.6.

On WMT 2014 the big Transformer scored 28.4 BLEU English-German (more than 2 BLEU over the best previous results including ensembles) and 41.8 English-French; the base model (27.3) beat every previous single model and ensemble (best 26.36). Base trained in 12 hours (100K steps) and big in 3.5 days (300K steps) on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.
By the paper's own estimates the base Transformer's training cost 3.3e18 FLOPs against 2.3e19 for Google's GNMT+RL, about one-seventh (a derived ratio).
Version 7 of the paper contains two English-French figures: 41.8 BLEU in the abstract and Table 2, and 41.0 in the text of section 6.1; the film should use 41.8 or omit the number.

The paper's Table 1 gives self-attention O(n^2 d) cost per layer with O(1) sequential operations and O(1) maximum path length, versus O(n) for both in recurrent layers; self-attention is cheaper than recurrence when sequence length n is smaller than representation size d, and its n^2 cost led the authors to float restricted local attention for long inputs.
A 4-layer Transformer reached 91.3 F1 on WSJ constituency parsing trained on about 40K sentences and 92.7 semi-supervised, an experiment Kaiser added to show the model was not just a translator.

Two weeks after the 3 a.m. conversation, with Gomez back in Toronto, Kaiser emailed him 'Generated Wikipedia Articles': a transformer given two days to read 'a little less than half' of Wikipedia had invented five plausible articles titled 'The Transformer', including a Japanese hardcore-punk band 'formed in 1968'. Gomez: 'I was shocked, blown away'.

Google's research blog announced the Transformer on 31 August 2017 (by Jakob Uszkoreit) and open-sourced Tensor2Tensor; it said that for 'I arrived at the bank after crossing the river' the model 'can learn to immediately attend to the word river'.

At the NIPS 2017 poster session in Long Beach on 6 December 2017 the crowd stayed until the 10:30 pm close ('Security had to tell us to leave'), and Sepp Hochreiter, co-inventor of the LSTM, praised the work.

The paper's Figures 3-5 show layer-5 encoder heads attending from 'making' to the distant 'more difficult', and two heads 'apparently involved in anaphora resolution' with attentions 'very sharp' for 'its'; the caption says 'The heads clearly learned to perform different tasks.'

Liu et al. (including Kaiser and Shazeer), 'Generating Wikipedia by Summarizing Long Sequences' (arXiv 30 January 2018), introduced 'a decoder-only architecture'; OpenAI's GPT-1 says it uses 'a multi-layer Transformer decoder [34]', citing that Google paper.

ELMo (Allen Institute for AI and University of Washington, arXiv 15 February 2018) used a 2-layer bidirectional LSTM, not a transformer, and was a NAACL 2018 Outstanding Paper; it was not the first pretrained contextual model, since CoVe (1 August 2017) and ULMFiT (18 January 2018) came earlier.

In spring 2018 Shazeer gave a talk titled 'Bigger Is Better' on scaling transformers; per Wired he had proposed that Google replace its search index with one huge transformer, an idea Kaiser at the time thought ridiculous.

OpenAI's GPT-1 (blog 11 June 2018; Radford, Narasimhan, Salimans, Sutskever) was a 12-layer decoder-only Transformer (768-dim, 12 heads) pretrained on BooksCorpus ('over 7,000 unique unpublished books') at a cost of '1 month on 8 GPUs', then fine-tuned, setting state of the art on 9 of 12 tasks.

Google's BERT (arXiv 11 October 2018; Devlin, Chang, Lee, Toutanova) was a bidirectional encoder-only Transformer (110M base, 340M large) trained by masking 15% of tokens on BooksCorpus plus English Wikipedia (3.3B words); it set records on eleven tasks (GLUE 80.4 in the October 2018 v1; 80.5 in the May 2019 v2); each pretraining took 4 days on up to 64 TPU chips; BERT-base was sized to match OpenAI GPT.

OpenAI announced GPT-2 on 14 February 2019: a 1.5-billion-parameter (paper: 1542M, 48 layers) decoder-only model trained to predict the next word on WebText, 40 GB from about 8 million web pages linked from Reddit posts with at least 3 karma; it reached state of the art on 7 of 8 language-modelling datasets zero-shot.

OpenAI withheld the full GPT-2 citing 'concerns about malicious applications' and released it in stages: a model it called '345M' in May 2019 (relabelled 355M by August), 774M on 20 August 2019 and the full 1.5B on 5 November 2019, when it wrote 'We've seen no strong evidence of misuse so far'; Cornell partners measured human-rated credibility of 6.91 (1.5B), 6.72 (774M) and 6.07 (355M) out of 10.

The phrase 'too dangerous to release' does not appear in OpenAI's 14 February 2019 post; the Guardian's headline the same day was 'New AI fake text generator may be too dangerous to release, say creators'. Who originated the framing is contested; safe wording is 'the press framed it as too dangerous to release'.

The Verge (21 February 2019) reported the backlash: Anima Anandkumar said withholding GPT-2 'put academics at a big disadvantage', Delip Rao said 'too dangerous' was 'casually thrown out', and OpenAI's Miles Brundage replied that 'it's important to distinguish what we said from what others said'.

OpenAI's GPT-2 post showcased a completion of a human-written prompt about 'a herd of unicorns living in a remote, previously unexplored valley, in the Andes Mountains' who 'spoke perfect English'; the post notes the sample took '10 tries'.
Google's T5 (arXiv 23 October 2019) cast every task as text-to-text, trained on the about-750 GB C4 corpus from Common Crawl, with models up to 11 billion parameters on TPU v3 pod slices.

On 25 October 2019 Google said BERT was helping it understand 'one in 10 searches in the U.S. in English', calling it 'the biggest leap forward in the past five years'; per Wired, Google had moved Translate to transformers in 2018.

Whether attention weights explain a model was debated: Jain and Wallace, 'Attention is not Explanation' (arXiv 26 February 2019, mostly on BiLSTM-with-attention classifiers); Clark et al. found BERT heads tracking syntax and coreference 'with remarkably high accuracy' (11 June 2019); Wiegreffe and Pinter replied 'Attention is not not Explanation' (13 August 2019).

Anthropic's Elhage et al., 'A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits' (22 December 2021), first named and described induction heads, a two-head circuit completing [A][B]...[A] -> [B]; Olsson et al. (8 March 2022) showed they form in a sudden phase change visible as a bump in training loss and may be 'the mechanism for the actual majority of all in-context learning in large transformer models', on evidence they call 'preliminary and indirect'.

Every ingredient of the Transformer had precedents (Bahdanau attention 2014, intra-attention 2016-17, residual connections, layer normalisation by Ba, Kiros and Hinton 2016); the paper's own claim is narrower: 'the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention'.

Juergen Schmidhuber argues 1991-era 'fast weight programmers' are equivalent to linear (unnormalised) self-attention (Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber 2021); mainstream credit for softmax self-attention and the 2017 architecture goes to Vaswani et al. Present as a claim, not a settled priority.

Whether Google 'missed' its own invention is disputed: Sam Altman told Wired 'I don't think anyone at Google realized what it meant' and Uszkoreit asked 'why didn't we do anything with the fact that we had seen it?'; on the other side Google shipped transformers in Translate (2018) and BERT in Search (2019).

Jakob Uszkoreit's father, the computational linguist Hans Uszkoreit, had been jailed for 15 months in East Germany for protesting the 1968 Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia; he doubted self-attention at the dinner table and later co-founded a company building language models 'using transformers, of course'.
Google colleague Mat Kelcey, who told Llion Jones about self-attention, doubted it would work: 'basically the biggest incorrect prediction of my life'.

By March 2024 all eight authors had left Google (Wired): Gomez co-founded Cohere (Toronto, 2019); Shazeer co-founded Character.AI (October 2021); Vaswani and Parmar co-founded Adept then Essential AI; Jones co-founded Sakana AI (Tokyo); Uszkoreit co-founded Inceptive (RNA biotech); Polosukhin co-founded NEAR; Kaiser joined OpenAI, the only one not to found a company.

Google rehired Shazeer from Character.AI in a licensing deal announced 2 August 2024 and he became a Gemini co-lead; Reuters, CNBC and Axios headlines of 17-18 June 2026 report he left Google for OpenAI. Cohere announced a merger with Germany's Aleph Alpha in April 2026 and signed it on 16 September 2026. Outlets reported in February-March 2025 that Parmar had joined Anthropic (start date unverified). All headline-level.

'Concrete Problems in AI Safety' (arXiv 21 June 2016) by Amodei, Olah, Steinhardt, Christiano, Schulman and Mane set out practical accident risks in machine learning; Anthropic later cited it as prior team work.

Bard opened 21 March 2023; Google announced Gemini on 6 December 2023 and renamed Bard Gemini on 8 February 2024.

Meta released LLaMA (7B-65B, trained on 1.4 trillion tokens of public data) to researchers on request on 24 February 2023; on 3 March 2023 its weights leaked via a torrent link posted on 4chan, and the same day someone opened a pull request to add the magnet link to Meta's official GitHub README.

OpenAI announced GPT-4 on 14 March 2023, a 'large multimodal model' (image and text in, text out); its report gave a simulated Uniform Bar Exam score of 298/400 (~90th percentile) vs 213/400 (~10th) for GPT-3.5, LSAT 163 (~88th), SAT Math 700 (~89th), GRE Verbal 169 (~99th, GPT-3.5 154), and said performance was predicted from runs using 1,000x-10,000x less compute, while giving 'no further details about the architecture (including model size), hardware, training compute, dataset construction, training method, or similar'.

GPT-4's ~90th-percentile bar figure is contested: Eric Martinez (Artificial Intelligence and Law, 30 March 2024) argued it was skewed by February repeat test-takers and estimated GPT-4 at ~62nd percentile against first-time takers (~42nd on essays) and ~48th among those who passed (~15th on essays).

Anthropic launched Claude and Claude Instant on 14 March 2023, the same day OpenAI announced GPT-4, after a closed alpha with Notion, Quora and DuckDuckGo; it followed with Claude 2 (11 July 2023), the Claude 3 family Haiku/Sonnet/Opus (4 March 2024), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (page dated 21 June 2024) and an upgraded 3.5 Sonnet with a 'computer use' beta (22 October 2024).

Microsoft Research's 'Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence' (Bubeck and 13 co-authors, arXiv 22 March 2023) probed a pre-release GPT-4 with informal tasks (stacking a book, nine eggs, a laptop, a bottle and a nail; drawing a unicorn in TikZ) and argued it 'could reasonably be viewed as an early (yet still incomplete) version of an artificial general intelligence (AGI) system'; critics including Maarten Sap and Alison Gopnik called it PR and anthropomorphism, noting the authors' own admission their approach was subjective and informal.

The Future of Life Institute's open letter (dated 22 March 2023, publicised 28-29 March) called on labs to 'immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4'; signers included Bengio, Stuart Russell, Elon Musk, Steve Wozniak and Yuval Noah Harari; the online count reached 31,810 (the NYT reported 'more than 1,000 technology leaders and researchers' at the time). Eliezer Yudkowsky said it 'doesn't go far enough'; no major lab paused.

On 31 March 2023 three listed authors of Stochastic Parrots (Gebru, Bender, McMillan-Major, per the DAIR byline) said the pause letter's recommendations 'are overshadowed by fearmongering and AI hype' and that its hypothetical risks were the focus of 'a dangerous ideology called longtermism'; Margaret Mitchell criticised the letter separately to Reuters.

The New York Times (Cade Metz, 1 May 2023), interviewing him in the dining room of his Toronto home, reported Geoffrey Hinton had quit Google to speak about AI risks; Hinton tweeted that he left 'so that I could talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google. Google has acted very responsibly.' He told the BBC (2 May) he did not back a pause: 'China would just get a big lead'.

Hinton told the NYT in May 2023 that he had thought smarter-than-human AI was '30 to 50 years or even longer away. Obviously, I no longer think that.'; the NYT wrote that 'a part of him' now regretted his life's work.

On 30 May 2023 the Center for AI Safety published a one-sentence statement: 'Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.' Hinton was the first listed signatory and Bengio second; Hassabis, Altman and Dario Amodei also signed.

At a Meta press event in Paris (BBC, 14-15 June 2023) Yann LeCun called fears that a super-intelligent system would 'take over the world within minutes' 'preposterously ridiculous', said it would run 'on a data centre somewhere with an off switch', and (in BBC reported speech) that human-level AI was years if not decades away.

The 2023 risk debate split three ways: existential-risk worriers (CAIS, FLI, Hinton, Bengio, Yudkowsky), present-harms critics (the DAIR authors), and sceptics of doom (LeCun); the three 2018 Turing laureates split two (Hinton, Bengio) to one (LeCun). People also overlapped: Hinton named bad actors and job loss as well as takeover.

Anthropic published its Responsible Scaling Policy on 19 September 2023, defining AI Safety Levels 'modeled loosely after the US government's biosafety level (BSL) standards', from ASL-1 (no meaningful catastrophic risk) to ASL-3 (substantially increased risk of catastrophic misuse or low-level autonomous capabilities).

Amazon agreed on 25 September 2023 to invest up to $4 billion in Anthropic ($1.25 billion initially, $2.75 billion more on 27 March 2024) and a further $4 billion on 22 November 2024, totalling $8 billion as a minority investor, with AWS as primary cloud and training partner; Google agreed in October 2023 to invest $500 million upfront and $1.5 billion over time (per an Anthropic spokesperson to Reuters, 27 October 2023). Earlier, in April 2022, Anthropic's $580 million round included $500 million from FTX; Anthropic was not implicated in FTX's fraud.

Anthropic's 'Towards Monosemanticity' (4 October 2023) used sparse autoencoders on a one-layer transformer's 512-neuron MLP (8 billion data points, up to 131,072 features) to address polysemantic neurons caused by 'superposition'; 'Scaling Monosemanticity' (21 May 2024) found up to ~34 million features in Claude 3 Sonnet, including a Golden Gate Bridge feature that also fired on images though learned from text; 'Golden Gate Claude' was online as a research demo for 24 hours from 23 May 2024.

President Biden signed Executive Order 14110 on 30 October 2023, requiring reports on models trained with more than 10^26 operations (10^23 for models trained mainly on biological sequences) and on clusters above 10^20 operations per second; it was revoked on 20 January 2025 by EO 14148.

The Bletchley Declaration (AI Safety Summit, Bletchley Park, 1-2 November 2023), a political declaration rather than a treaty, was signed by 28 countries and the EU including both the United States and China, warning of 'potential for serious, even catastrophic, harm'; New Zealand joined on 23 October 2024.

The European Parliament adopted the EU AI Act on 13 March 2024 (523-46-49); it was published as Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on 12 July 2024 and entered into force on 1 August 2024, applying in phases (bans from 2 February 2025); it has four risk tiers plus general-purpose AI rules, presuming 'systemic risk' above 10^25 training FLOPs.

China's Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services (CAC Order No. 15; seven agencies; 24 articles) were published 13 July 2023 and took effect 15 August 2023; they apply to services offered to the public in the PRC, state 'equal weight to development and security' (Art. 3) and require adherence to 'core socialist values' (Art. 4).

On Friday 17 November 2023 OpenAI's board removed Sam Altman, saying he 'was not consistently candid in his communications with the board'; Mira Murati became interim CEO and Greg Brockman quit. Emmett Shear was named interim CEO on 19 November; on 20 November Microsoft said it would hire Altman, a staff letter reportedly signed by 745 of 770 employees demanded the board resign, and Ilya Sutskever signed and publicly apologised; an 'agreement in principle' late on 21 November (Pacific) returned Altman with a new board of Bret Taylor (chair), Larry Summers and Adam D'Angelo.

Why Altman was removed remains disputed: the board's only public reason was candour; later reporting cites concerns over safety, commercialisation and candour (including that employee concerns were led by Sutskever and Murati, which was not public in November 2023); Helen Toner said in May 2024 that Altman had withheld information; the WilmerHale review (March 2024) found his conduct 'did not mandate removal'; 'Q*' speculation was never confirmed.

Hinton learned of his share of the 2024 Physics Nobel (with John Hopfield, then 91) at about 2 a.m. in 'a cheap hotel in California' with no internet, had planned an MRI that day, and first wondered whether it was 'a spoof call'; committee chair Ellen Moons said the laureates 'used fundamental concepts from statistical physics', while Dame Wendy Hall called it 'a bit of a stretch'.

Whether the 2024 Physics Nobel was 'physics' was debated: the committee pointed to the Hopfield network's energy function and the Boltzmann machine's statistical physics; Wendy Hall asked whether the work was 'the result of physics research'. The prize was for associative memory and Boltzmann-machine work, not for transformers or LLMs.

The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (9 October 2024) went half to David Baker 'for computational protein design' and half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper 'for protein structure prediction' (AlphaFold), whose predictions cover 'virtually all the 200 million proteins' identified and were used by more than two million people in 190 countries.

In his Nobel banquet speech in Stockholm on 10 December 2024 Hinton warned of 'a longer term existential threat that will arise when we create digital beings that are more intelligent than ourselves'.

China's State Council completed its New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan on 8 July 2017 and released it on 20 July 2017, with three steps: keep pace with advanced levels by 2020 (core AI industry >150 billion RMB), major basic-theory breakthroughs by 2025 (>400 billion RMB), and 'world-leading levels' by 2030, 'making China the world's primary AI innovation center' (core industry >1 trillion RMB); the plan names no rival.

On 7 October 2022 the US Commerce Department's BIS issued controls on advanced computing chips, chipmaking equipment and 'U.S. persons' supporting advanced Chinese fabs, aiming to 'restrict the People's Republic of China's (PRC's) ability to both purchase and manufacture certain high-end chips used in military applications' (phased effect 7/12/21 October).

On 8 October 2022 PRC Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said (AP translation) the US 'abuses export control measures to maliciously block and suppress Chinese companies' out of 'the need to maintain its sci-tech hegemony'.

Nvidia answered the 2022 rules with China-specific variants with reduced chip-to-chip bandwidth (A800, H800); Dario Amodei confirms 'H800's were allowed under the initial round of 2022 export controls, but were banned in Oct 2023'.

BIS tightened the rules on 17 October 2023 to 'close loopholes', catching the A800/H800 and extending licence requirements to more countries; the scheduled effective date was 17 November, but on 23 October the US told Nvidia the requirement was 'effective immediately' for the A100, A800, H100, H800 and L40S (Nvidia 8-K). Gina Raimondo said on a 16 October press call the rules would be updated 'at least annually'; China's commerce ministry accused the US of 'unilateral bullying'.
On 2 December 2024 BIS added controls on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and more chipmaking tools, new foreign-direct-product rules, and 140 Entity List additions.

The Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion (announced 13 January 2025, published 15 January as 90 FR 4544) sorted countries into three tiers, for the first time controlled the weights of closed models trained with at least 10^26 operations (ECCN 4E091) while exempting open-weight models, and set compliance for 15 May 2025; BIS announced its rescission on 13 May 2025, saying it would have 'stifled American innovation', and the same day warned that using Huawei Ascend 910B/910C/910D chips 'anywhere in the world' risked violating US rules.

In April 2025 the US put Nvidia's China-specific H20 under an indefinite licence requirement (Nvidia warned of about $5.5 billion in charges); on 14 July 2025 Nvidia said the government 'has assured NVIDIA that licenses will be granted'; in August 2025 Nvidia and AMD agreed to pay the US 15% of China revenue from such chips, which Bloomberg called 'unusual and legally questionable'.

Beijing pushed back on Nvidia: the CAC summoned it on 31 July 2025 over alleged H20 'back door' risks (Nvidia denied any); China's market regulator SAMR said on 15 September 2025 that preliminary findings showed Nvidia violated anti-monopoly law over Mellanox; and around 17 September the CAC reportedly told ByteDance, Alibaba and others to stop buying Nvidia's RTX Pro 6000D.

On 8 December 2025 President Trump said Nvidia's H200 could go to approved Chinese customers with 25% to the US; BIS issued a case-by-case rule on 13 January 2026 (effective 15 January); on 14 January Reuters reported Chinese customs had told agents the H200 was 'not permitted'; on 28 January Beijing gave conditional, preliminary approval for ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent to buy more than 400,000 H200s; in mid-March Nvidia said it had licences for 'many customers'; yet on 14 May 2026 Reuters reported about 10 Chinese firms had US approval but not a single H200 had been delivered.
The US Justice Department announced 'Operation Gatekeeper' on 8 December 2025, documenting at least $160 million of H100/H200 smuggling between October 2024 and May 2025.

On 23 February 2026 a senior US administration official told Reuters DeepSeek's coming model had been trained on Nvidia Blackwell chips, likely in Inner Mongolia ('we're not shipping Blackwells to China'); the Chinese embassy rejected the claim, no public proof was presented, and December 2025 'ghost data center' smuggling reports were called 'far-fetched' by Nvidia. An allegation, not an established fact.

Alibaba open-sourced Qwen-7B on 3 August 2023; by October 2025 Qwen had passed Meta's Llama in cumulative Hugging Face downloads (Alibaba/Xinhua citing Hugging Face data, with the independent ATOM report showing the same trend).

DeepSeek-V3's technical report (GitHub 26 December 2024; arXiv 27 December UTC) describes a 671B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (37B active per token) trained on 14.8 trillion tokens on 'a cluster equipped with 2048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs' for 2.788 million GPU-hours, which 'Assuming the rental price of the H800 GPU is $2 per GPU hour' totals '$5.576M', 'excluding the costs associated with prior research and ablation experiments'.

DeepSeek released R1 on 20 January 2025 under the MIT licence with six distilled small models; that same day founder Liang Wenfeng, then 40, attended Premier Li Qiang's symposium, reportedly the only AI executive there.

On 27 January 2025, after the DeepSeek app topped the US App Store's free list (the company also reported a 'large-scale' cyberattack and limited registrations), Nvidia fell about 17% and lost $589 billion (Bloomberg) or $593 billion (Reuters/LSEG) in market value, the largest one-day loss in US market history; the Nasdaq fell 3.1%, the Philadelphia semiconductor index 9.2%, ASML 7% and SoftBank 8.3%.

Whether DeepSeek 'cost $6 million' is disputed: the paper's $5.576M was the rental-equivalent price of the final V3 run and excluded research; SemiAnalysis estimated access to about 50,000 Hopper GPUs and about $1.6 billion in server capex; Amodei wrote DeepSeek did not 'do for $6M what cost US AI companies billions' and put Claude 3.5 Sonnet's training at 'a few $10M's'; defenders note DeepSeek never claimed the whole programme cost $6M.

In 'On DeepSeek and Export Controls' (January 2025) Dario Amodei wrote that DeepSeek produced a model 'close to the performance of US models 7-10 months older', that V3 was 'not a unique breakthrough', that well-enforced export controls decide whether the world is unipolar or 'bipolar' in AI, and 'I don't see DeepSeek themselves as adversaries'.

Chinese labs kept releasing open weights: Baidu open-sourced ERNIE 4.5 (30 June 2025), Moonshot released Kimi K2 (1 trillion parameters, 32B active, 11 July 2025), Zhipu released GLM-4.5 (28 July 2025), and Alibaba released Qwen3.5-397B-A17B under Apache-2.0 (15-16 February 2026).

DeepSeek released a V4 preview on 24 April 2026: V4-Pro (1.6 trillion total, 49B active) and V4-Flash (284B total, 13B active), 1-million-token context, MIT licence, adapted for Huawei Ascend; how much of its training used Ascend is undisclosed.

Huawei's Ascend 910B/910C are made on SMIC's enhanced 7 nm-class process (Nvidia's comparable chips use TSMC 4 nm); on 18 September 2025 rotating chairman Eric Xu announced a roadmap - Ascend 950PR (Q1 2026), 950DT (Q4 2026), 960 (Q4 2027), 970 (Q4 2028) - promising to 'double compute with each release', with supernodes of 8,192 and 15,488 chips, while conceding China would lag in process nodes for a long time; SemiAnalysis reports poor large-die yields.

MacroPolo's Global AI Talent Tracker 2.0 (NeurIPS 2022 authors as a proxy for the top tier) found 47% did their undergraduate degree in China, up from 29% in 2019, against 18% in the US; the US remained the leading place they worked, hosting about 60% of top AI institutions; Brookings notes undergraduate coding may understate China-origin researchers.
At the Woodside summit on 15 November 2023 Presidents Biden and Xi 'affirmed the need to address the risks of advanced AI systems and improve AI safety through U.S.-China government talks'.

The first US-China intergovernmental AI dialogue was held in Geneva on 14 May 2024 (led for the US by Tarun Chhabra and Seth Center); the US raised 'misuse of AI, including by the PRC' and China 'expressed a stern stance on the U.S. restrictions and pressure'; Singapore's RSIS called the bar 'low'.
In Lima on 16 November 2024 Biden and Xi 'affirmed the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons', the first such joint statement.

The International Dialogues on AI Safety (convened by Bengio, Andrew Yao, Stuart Russell and Zhang Ya-Qin) met at Ditchley Park (31 October 2023), the Aman Summer Palace in Beijing (10-11 March 2024; red lines; attended and signed by three Turing laureates, Yao, Hinton and Bengio), Casa dei Tre Oci in Venice (5-8 September 2024; 'AI safety as a global public good'), Shanghai (22-25 July 2025) and the Royal Society, London (17-19 April 2026). Hinton attended Beijing and Shanghai and signed the Beijing and Venice statements but was not a convener.

The White House released 'Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan' on 23 July 2025 ('We need to ensure America has leading open models founded on American values'); three days later, on 26 July at the World AI Conference in Shanghai, Premier Li Qiang announced China's Global AI Governance Action Plan and proposed a World AI Cooperation Organization, which Xi proposed again at APEC on 1 November 2025.
On 5 September 2025 Anthropic barred companies more than 50% owned by entities in unsupported regions, including China, from using Claude.

On 23 February 2026 Anthropic said it had detected 'industrial-scale' distillation of Claude by DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax via about 24,000 fraudulent accounts and more than 16 million exchanges (DeepSeek >150,000; Moonshot >3.4M; MiniMax >13M); on 8 September 2026 an NSA/CISA/FBI advisory (AA26-251A) alleged industrial-scale distillation by Chinese labs; China's foreign ministry called these 'unfounded accusations or smears' and its commerce ministry said distillation 'is a common practice' and threatened 'resolute countermeasures'. Allegations, contested.

Trump visited Beijing on 14-15 May 2026, discussing AI 'guardrails' and chips without a formal AI agreement; Xi made a state visit to Washington on 23-25 September 2026, where the two sides agreed an AI dialogue (the White House's 'U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue', Beijing's 'China-U.S. AI Dialogue') with its next exchange by November 2026 and a channel for AI incidents; chip export controls were unchanged.

Estimates of the US-China gap vary: Liang Wenfeng (July 2024) said people speak of 'a gap of one or two years' but the real gap is 'between originality and imitation'; Amodei (January 2025) said 7-10 months; Hassabis told CNBC (16 January 2026) Chinese models may be 'only a matter of months' behind and Bloomberg at Davos (20 January) about six months, calling the R1 reaction a 'massive overreaction'; Jensen Huang said on BG2 (26 September 2025) China was 'nanoseconds behind' in chips; Qwen's Lin Junyang (about 10 January 2026) put the chance of a Chinese firm overtaking US giants in 3-5 years under 20%, citing compute.

Whether export controls work is disputed: Amodei and former NSC official Saif Khan argue they are decisive and that reliance on smuggled chips shows a domestic shortfall; Jensen Huang (with a commercial interest in China sales) argues restrictions hand the market to Huawei; China's foreign ministry says they will 'only hurt and isolate' the US; Beijing's own purchase restrictions suggest controls also hardened Chinese self-reliance policy.

OpenAI released o1-preview and o1-mini on 12 September 2024, models trained with large-scale RL to produce a long hidden chain of thought (hidden 'by design'); the headline AIME 2024 results (74% single-sample, 83% with consensus of 64) and 89th-percentile Codeforces were for the full o1, unreleased that day, while o1-preview scored about 56.7% (cons@64) and the 62nd percentile, against GPT-4o's 12%. The full o1 was released on 5 December 2024.
